parsed.explanation: Nothing criminalises trans identity and no visitor-facing exposure is documented; entry, passport markers, screening, facilities, custody and detention placement are explicitly unsourced, so they are open questions, not exposures (rules 13, 15). But the record is thin and self-consciously undercounts, so silence is not safety (rule 3). Known negatives: a historic morality ordinance reported in force in one region (in-force status contested) carrying up to ten years; public-morality provisions reaching trans people; police documented arresting and torturing queer residents and banning LGBTQ organising; no non-discrimination or complaint route; very low social acceptance, with family/public abuse reported; HIV medication access precarious. The same-sex statute and resident-scoped enforcement are secondary (rule 2) and undated (rule 18), and the 12-person 2018 sample cannot establish trans-specific prevalence (rule 17). One step below acceptance-with-protections; a weak tier-2/strong tier-3 profile.
